# Homographies {#sec-homography}

## Introduction

In @sec-geometry_homogeneous we discussed several types of
geometric transformations of two-dimensional (2D) images: translations,
rotations, skewing, scalings, and we saw that all could be modeled as
the product between the coordinates of a point in the input image
described using homogeneous coordinates and a $3 \times 3$ matrix. Now
that we have discussed camera models, we are well equipped to present a
more general geometric image transformation that opens the door to many
applications: the homography.

As we discussed in the previous @sec-stereo_vision, if we capture a scene with two cameras
from different viewpoints, corresponding points across both images are
constrained by the epipolar constrain. In general, there is not a simple
geometric transformation that maps pixels from one image into the pixels
of the other image. To find that mapping we will need to know the
three-dimensional (3D) location of each point as well as the relative
camera translation and rotation between both images.

However, there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple
transformation that allows warping one image into another image
corresponding to a new camera location without requiring knowing the 3D
scene structure: this will happen when the scene is planar (as in
@fig-illustration_homography) or when the two cameras are related just
by a rotation (@fig-rotation_homography). In those two cases the
coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by
a **homography**.


:::{#fig-illustration_homography layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/homography/IMG_7801_crop.jpg){width="45%"}

![](figures/homography/IMG_7802_crop.jpg){width="48%"}

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography.
:::

elements: Origin optical center (small black sphere at [0, 0, 0])
Green coordinate axis Y pointing vertically up from origin with label 'Y'
Green coordinate axis X pointing diagonally up-right from origin with label 'X'
Green coordinate axis Z pointing diagonally down-right from origin with label 'Z'
Camera 1 image plane (semi-transparent green rectangle) positioned in front of the camera center
Camera 2 image plane (semi-transparent red rectangle) sharing the same center but rotated by angle R
Text label 'Camera 1' positioned next to the green plane
Text label 'Camera 2' positioned next to the red plane
Two black projection rays originating from the optical center, passing through both the green and red planes
Green intersection points (dots) where the rays pierce the Camera 1 plane
Red intersection points (dots) where the rays pierce the Camera 2 plane
Dotted projection lines continuing past the planes into space
Curved black arrow 'R' at the top showing the rotational transition from Camera 1 to Camera 2

interactions.label: Rotation (R)
interactions.teaches: Rotating the camera around its optical center warps the image plane projection without changing the center of projection, demonstrating a pure rotational homography.

interactions.label: Project Ray
interactions.teaches: Dragging the ray demonstrates that every point on Camera 1 maps to exactly one point on Camera 2, independent of scene depth.

demo_steps.title: Shared Optical Center
demo_steps.narration: Observe that both Camera 1 (green) and Camera 2 (red) share the exact same optical center at the origin. Because there is zero translation between them, the 3D depth of the scene does not cause any parallax.

demo_steps.title: Rotational Misalignment
demo_steps.narration: As Camera 2 rotates by angle R, the rays from the shared center intersect the two planes at different physical coordinates. This spatial warping is described perfectly by a 3x3 homography matrix.

demo_steps.title: One-to-One Pixel Mapping
demo_steps.narration: Trace the light rays from the origin. Since both planes intersect the same rays, any pixel in Camera 1 has a unique, direct corresponding pixel in Camera 2, enabling perfect image stitching or warping without knowing 3D scene depth.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An orthographic view from the front-left, slightly elevated, looking down the diagonal towards the image planes to clearly separate the shared origin from the dual planes.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant directional structure is the set of projection rays running from the lower-left foreground (optical center) to the upper-right background (image planes). (2) This receding diagonal structure implies an azimuth angle of approximately -35 degrees to place the camera broadside to the projection rays, allowing us to see the depth separation. (3) The top edges of both planes tilt slightly downward to the right, showing a moderate elevation cue of about 15 degrees above the horizontal plane.

camera_view.view_notes: Positioned to perfectly replicate the textbook perspective where the coordinate origin is in the lower-left, and the two intersecting planes sweep across the center and right side of the frame.

inline_constraints.framing: maintain comfortable margin around the green and red planes to prevent edge clipping
inline_constraints.camera: must match the exact oblique perspective of the source diagram at first load

The rotation parameter should dynamically update the orientation of the red plane, its label, and its corresponding ray intersection dots.
